k-1.x_notes: Strengths: outlines are true actual size (rhombus, trapezoid, pennant check out at 1-inch edges); the pennant (side-2 triangle on a half-hexagon, 7 triangles) does have several fillings (yellow+green, red+red+green, red+blue+2 greens), and the footer matches the organizer's format. Weaknesses: only two pages; Problems 1 and 2 are one-block placements that take a minute each (exactly the 'too dumbed down, ends too early' complaint); after the pennant the remaining work is an unnumbered 'Play shop with a partner' game and a 'Tell or show' reflection box. Name/Date fields, extra page titles ('The block exchange shop', 'Same outside, new inside'), 'An adult can read these prompts aloud', 'Build first...' line and an adult printing note all sit on the student page. K-1 children would run out of material well before 40 minutes.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: five numbered problems on actual-size boards (hexagons 2 in, star 3 in across, triangles of side 2/3/4 at 2, 3, 4 in), building from counting greens on each block, to six hexagon boards for 'fill a new way' (many fillings, including chevron+blue), to stars (Star 2 with blues only has exactly one tiling, 6 blues, and the prompt asks whether there is more than one), to big triangles 4/9/16 with the 2x/3x upscale blocks, to a K-1 entry into kernel 1: blues plus fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3, 4 gives 2, 3, 4, with 'what do you notice?'. Correct mathematics and plenty of hands-on work for the whole period. Weaknesses: Name field; 'Talk about it' boxes and a 'Your turn!' box are adult prompts on the student page; some cutesy exclamations ('Cover it all up!'); dashed grid lines let children count triangles without building; footer is a print note, not the organizer's id footer.
k-1.reason: X's K-1 pages are two trivial placements plus one pennant and a vague game, so the band would finish in about ten minutes. Y gives five substantial, correct, actual-size building problems that work up to the up/down packing idea at a K-1 level. Its format problems take a few minutes to edit out.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: actual-size outlines; puzzles are correct (pennant: yellow+green vs 2 blues+1 red works; double hexagon: 2 yellows vs 4 reds, or with no yellow, 4 reds vs 6 blues). Weaknesses: ignores the outline's kernel 1 entirely (no possible/impossible boards, no up/down counting, no fewest-gap packings); the 'no shared colors' puzzle is shallow, because single-color fillings solve Problems 2 and 3 almost at once; Problems 2 and 3 reuse the same double-hexagon outline, so there is little variety; only three problems. Internal labels leak ('The pennant / P1', 'Double hexagon / P2'), there are Name/Date fields and cutesy page titles ('Yellow takes a break'), the rule box is repeated on every page, 'Keep exploring:', 'Partner puzzle:' and 'If you want another puzzle:' labels stand in for tasks, and 'Build first...' appears on the page. The band would likely run short of real work.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: a faithful, well-sequenced development of kernel 1 on actual-size boards. The up/down table for each block (green and red give two answers, blue always 1+1, chevron 2+2) leads to possible/impossible boards. I checked the answers: A side-2 triangle 3 vs 1 is impossible; B is a 2-1-1 hexagon at 5/5 and possible; C is an inverted trapezoid at 3 vs 5 and impossible; D is a star at 6/6 and possible, all with even area. Broken hexagons: X removes two up-triangles (10 vs 12, impossible); I verified that Y (11/11) has an explicit tiling. Then fewest-gap triangles of side 3, 4, 5 with a table predicting sides 6 and 10 (up/down counts 21/15 and 55/45, n greens), and the purple chevron question. There is plenty of rich work for the full time. Weaknesses: Problem 1 is split into directed sub-steps and front-loads the up/down marking; hints give away the thinking ('Are they up or down?', 'leaves only as many gaps as the side length', '(Hint: each blue covers one up and one down)'); there are 'Talk about it', 'Make your own' and 'Purple puzzle' boxes, a Name field and exclamation marks.
grades-2-3.reason: Y develops the intended obstruction and packing mathematics correctly, with real contrasting boards. X substitutes a thin color-partition puzzle that third graders can dispatch with single-color fillings. Y's giveaway hints can be struck in a few minutes, but X's lack of content cannot be fixed in fifteen minutes.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: asks for minimality proofs, a genuine idea. Answers are correct and checkable: pennant minimum 5 (yellow+green, then red+2 blues); double hexagon 6 (2 yellows + 4 reds); with no yellow 10 (4 reds + 6 blues). Weaknesses: entirely misses kernel 2 (hexagon rhombus tilings, flips, ribbons); the optimizations reduce to quick area arithmetic and fall in perhaps 15 minutes for 4th-5th graders; two of three problems use the same outline. 'Think about:' lines hand over the argument ('What would a two-piece filling have to use?', 'what is the largest block the other copy can use?'). Name/Date fields, page titles, '/ P1' labels, repeated rule boxes and 'Build first' lines are on the page.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: an excellent, correct treatment of kernel 2 on actual-size boards (2-in hexagon, 3-in tall hexagon, 4-in big hexagon). The tall (1,2,2) hexagon has 6 = C(4,2) tilings, matching the ribbon words with two L and two R. The flip-map task is good; I decoded the given X and Y tilings as LLRR and RRLL, so the fewest flips is 4, provable by L-score. Round trips are always even via L-score parity. The big hexagon has two non-crossing ribbons and 20 tilings, with the link to comparable pairs in the flip map; the 3D cube view is included. It gives far more than enough for 40 minutes, with small recording hexagons for drawing tilings. Weaknesses: heavy sub-step numbering and reading load; some answers are given away ('There are exactly two ways', the L-score definition plus 'explain why a round trip can never have an odd number of flips' answers the round-trip question just asked); the cutesy 'Coming up... secret code' teaser box and the 'Tips' box with group roles and 'Stuck? ... flip them!' belong with the adult; Name field.
grades-4-5.reason: Y is a rich, correct, well-built investigation of exactly the intended mathematics; its flaws are giveaway lines and teaser boxes the organizer can cut quickly. X's fewest-pieces puzzles are correct but shallow, off-outline, and would leave the older children idle well before the hour ends.

overall.reason: In every band Y has correct, substantial, actual-size mathematics that follows the activity outline and keeps children building for the full working time. X is thin, repetitive and largely off-kernel: K-1 ends almost immediately, and 2-3 and 4-5 are reduced to an easy no-shared-colors puzzle. X's only edge is a cleaner header/footer; Y's format faults (Name field, talk boxes, a few giveaway hints and teaser lines) are quick to strike, while X's missing content cannot be written in fifteen minutes per band.
